I used to think good design was about making things look better.

The more products I build, the more I realize it's actually about making people's lives easier.

Over the past few months, I've been balancing engineering, running two brands, and now diving deeper into UX through the Google UX Design Professional Certificate.

One thing has become clear:

The best products aren't the ones with the most features. They're the ones that remove friction.

Whether it's an e-commerce checkout, a healthcare platform, or even a simple landing page, every extra click, confusing button, or unnecessary step is a chance to lose someone's trust.

That's the mindset I'm trying to develop. Not just building things that work, but building experiences that people genuinely enjoy using.

I'm excited to keep learning, applying these principles to real projects, and sharing the journey along the way.

What was one lesson that completely changed the way you think about design or building products?

#UXDesign #ProductDesign #GoogleUXDesign #DesignThinking #UserExperience #Tech

Webhooks are only as reliable as your error handling logic for failed deliveries. 

Earlier this month, I noticed our Razorpay integration missed two payment callbacks because of a brief network timeout. I had relied on the assumption that the response would always land perfectly on the first try. That assumption cost me a manual reconciliation of our financial logs against our bank statement. 

I ended up writing a secondary listener that periodically polls the API for missed events. It is not the most elegant solution, but it guarantees that our order status remains accurate.

My obsession with minimizing dependency bloat has changed how I ship software. 

When we were building the early internal tools for Prettiva, I kept adding npm packages for every minor requirement. I soon realized that our build times for the frontend were creeping past the four-minute mark on our local machines. I spent a weekend stripping out half of those libraries and writing native functions to handle tasks like date formatting and state management. 

It shaved our bundle size by 30 percent and made the codebase much easier to reason about. The best library is often the one you do not need to install. 

What is one dependency you regretted adding to your codebase? 

#javascript #webperformance #softwarearchitecture

Inventory management is not just about tracking items in a spreadsheet. 

It is about understanding how the front-end display logic interacts with the back-end database queries. When we were setting up variant tracking for STRAYED, I realized that simple table joins were killing our query performance. I had to restructure our data model to prioritize faster lookups for the specific variants we sell most often. 

It was a tough realization that our initial database design was not built for scale. Refactoring that mid-launch was the most stressful week of my life.

I used to ignore logs until a feature failed to show up in production. 

Early on, I relied on console logs to debug errors as I built, assuming everything would just work once it was deployed. That changed when a critical feature for our checkout flow broke without leaving any trace in the browser console. I spent six hours digging through our server access logs to find that an API response was returning an unexpected null value. 

Now, I spend as much time designing our error reporting as I do building the actual UI. A good logging system turns a nightmare debugging session into a simple five-minute fix. 

How do you handle observability for your personal projects? 

#debugging #softwareengineering #devops

Documentation is just as important as the code you write for yourself. 

Six months ago, I pushed a major update to our site and then took a week off from touching that specific module. When I came back to add a small feature, I spent an hour trying to decipher why I wrote a specific conditional logic block that way. I had no comments and zero documentation to explain my thought process. 

I realized that my future self is essentially a stranger who needs clear instructions. Now, I write brief documentation for every complex function I create. 

What habit do you use to keep your code maintainable for your future self? 

#programming #developer #documentation
pending.reasoning: Reflects on the personal impact of bad documentation, a common problem for solo or small-team developers.

I stopped testing my site only on high-end monitors a long time ago. 

Our usage data showed that a significant portion of our users access our store from budget devices with smaller screens. I started using a set of older Android phones to test our UI responsiveness because emulators do not capture how the hardware actually handles heavy JavaScript execution. I found that animations which looked fine on my laptop were causing a jittery experience on those devices. 

Building for the hardware people actually use is far more important than building for the hardware you own. 

How do you perform mobile-first testing for your own web projects? 

#uxdesign #mobileweb #webdevelopment
pending.reasoning: Addresses the practical reality of web development in a market like India where device variety is high.
